title: Layer Stacker
context: Grade 5, the pages on the volume of a cuboid and a cube and Exercise 8.4. An adult sees two formulas. What the pages are doing is shortening a count: the cubes in a layer times the number of layers give the count, so the volume of a cuboid is length x breadth x height, and a cube, a cuboid with all its edges equal, is side x side x side.

writeup.why: See that the cubes in a layer times the number of layers give the count, so the volume of a cuboid is length x breadth x height; tell a cube by all its edges equal; and multiply an edge in tenths by whole numbers.
writeup.look: A base layer of violet cubes with the Height handle beside it, the Edge checker on the third phase and the Tenths lens on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Layer Stacker' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of cubes stacked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The solid stands in three visible faces at x 160, y 260 inside a box 600 by 400, every unit cube 40 across, its length and breadth labelled deep blue along the base. The base layer is violet, labelled Layer. The Height handle is a round grip at the solid's right edge that the child drags upward; each layer it stacks lights amber for a moment. The Units switch stands at x 820, y 250. The Edge checker's bead runs along the length, the breadth and the height in turn, and the label Cube or Cuboid appears under the solid in ink. The Tenths lens is a round glass 90 across at x 820, y 400 that rewrites an edge in tenths as a count of tenths; a card at x 820, y 500 reads Taught later when two edges have tenths. The working line runs along y 690 from x 120. The volume reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key and cu. cm and cu. m keys. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last solid stands stacked with its layers, labelled Cube or Cuboid, and the volume in green with its cubic unit.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when all three edges light together, the solid gives a little spin on the spot and settles with the word Cube under it.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet stacked. On the first phase a base layer of cubes lies on the table top with the Height handle beside it. On the second a box lies with its edges labelled and the Units switch set. On the third a solid stands with the Edge checker's bead at one corner. On the fourth a box stands with one edge in tenths and the Tenths lens beside it. One thing moves, once: the Height handle, the Edge checker's bead or the Tenths lens gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any base, stacked to any height, checked for equal edges or read through the Tenths lens. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on layers, length x breadth x height, cubes and edges in tenths.

source_tool.description: A base layer of violet unit cubes, labelled Layer, is drawn in three visible faces, its length and breadth labelled deep blue. The child drags a Height handle upward, and each layer stacked lights amber for a moment and adds one layer's worth to the running count. A Units switch gives the edges centimetres or metres, and the product is then written length x breadth x height with a cubic unit. An Edge checker runs a bead along the length, the breadth and the height in turn; when all three edges are equal they light together and the solid is labelled Cube, and otherwise it is labelled Cuboid. On the last phase a Tenths lens held over an edge in tenths of a centimetre rewrites it as a count of tenths, and the working line multiplies that count by the whole-number edges and writes the answer back in cu. cm; when two edges have tenths the lens stays dark and a card reads Taught later. A number pad types a count or a volume with cu. cm and cu. m keys. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of cubes stacked.
source_tool.art_direction: Stacking sugar cubes on a tray / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count one layer, then count the layers again.
voice.onNext: A new box. Find one layer first.
voice.opening: A layer of cubes, ready to stack.
voice.onFinish: You turned stacking layers into length times breadth times height.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Stack layers on any base you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has built one layer of unit cubes, counted it, and stacked more layers by hand. The tool is what adds a layer's worth to the count each time a layer goes on, which the printed block shows only finished.

answer_key.rule: One layer has length x breadth cubes, and the layers stack up the height, so the volume of a cuboid is length x breadth x height; lengths in cm give cu. cm and lengths in m give cu. m. A cube is a cuboid with all its edges equal, so its volume is side x side x side; a solid with any two edges unequal is a cuboid, not a cube. An edge in tenths is a count of tenths: multiply the whole-number edges first, then the count of tenths, and write the answer back. When two edges both have tenths, the multiplying needs a step taught later.
answer_key.wrong: The child's layers stay stacked, and the stage counts them again one layer at a time beside the child's number, lighting amber the layer or the edge that differs. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

items.question: A cuboid is 7 cubes long, 5 cubes wide and 2 cubes high. How many cubes build it?
items.checkpoint: Cubes in one layer times the number of layers.
items.misconception: Adding the three counts, which gives the cubes along three edges, not the cubes that fill the cuboid.

steps: The volume of a cuboid is length x breadth x height.
So the volume of a cuboid 11 cm long, 6 cm wide and 4 cm high is 11 x 6 x 4 = 264 cu. cm.
Lengths in cm give a volume in cu. cm.
items.question: A box is 11 cm long, 6 cm wide and 4 cm high. What is its volume?
items.misconception: Multiplying only the length and the breadth, which gives one layer, not the whole box.

steps: All its edges are equal, so it is a cube.
The volume of a cube is side x side x side.
The volume of a cube of edge 9 cm is 9 x 9 x 9 = 729 cu. cm.
items.answer: Yes, it is a cube, and its volume is 729 cu. cm
items.question: A solid has edges of 9 cm, 9 cm and 9 cm. Is it a cube, and what is its volume?
items.checkpoint: A cube has all its edges equal.
items.misconception: Calling any box with a square face a cube, though a cube has all its edges equal.

steps: Multiply the whole numbers first: 8 x 2 = 16.
3.5 cm is 35 tenths of a cm, and 35 x 16 = 560.
So the volume is 560 tenths, which is 56 cu. cm.
So the volume of a cuboid 8 cm long, 3.5 cm wide and 2 cm high is 56 cu. cm.
items.question: A box is 8 cm long, 3.5 cm wide and 2 cm high. What is its volume?
items.checkpoint: Multiply the tenths by whole numbers, then write the answer back.
items.misconception: Forgetting that 35 counted tenths, and giving an answer ten times too big.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A cuboid is 7 cubes long, 2 cubes wide and 2 cubes high. How many cubes build it?
items.final_answer: One layer has 7 x 2 = 14 cubes, and 2 x 14 = 28, so 28 cubes

items.question: A box is 9 cm long, 7 cm wide and 2 cm high. What is its volume?
items.final_answer: The volume of a cuboid 9 cm long, 7 cm wide and 2 cm high is 9 x 7 x 2 = 126 cu. cm

items.question: A cube has edges of 10 m. What is its volume?
items.final_answer: The volume of a cube of edge 10 m is 10 x 10 x 10 = 1000 cu. m

items.question: A solid is 6 cm by 6 cm by 4 cm. Is it a cube?
items.final_answer: No. Its edges are not all equal, so it is a cuboid, not a cube

items.question: A tank is 11 m long, 5 m wide and 2 m high. What is its volume?
items.final_answer: The volume of a cuboid 11 m long, 5 m wide and 2 m high is 11 x 5 x 2 = 110 cu. m

items.question: A cuboid is 9 cubes long, 2 cubes wide and 3 cubes high. How many cubes build it?
items.final_answer: One layer has 9 x 2 = 18 cubes, and 3 x 18 = 54, so 54 cubes

items.question: A box is 6 cm long, 2.5 cm wide and 4 cm high. What is its volume?
items.final_answer: 6 x 4 = 24. 2.5 cm is 25 tenths, and 25 x 24 = 600, so 600 tenths, which is 60 cu. cm

items.question: A cuboid is 4 cm long, 2.5 cm wide and 1.5 cm high. Can its volume be found by multiplying tenths by whole numbers alone?
items.final_answer: No. Two of its edges have tenths, so it needs a decimal times a decimal, a step taught later

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Build one layer of unit cubes, count it, then stack more layers by hand before the tool opens. Layers times the cubes in a layer is the volume. Name the longer side of the base the length. A cube has all its edges equal; a solid with any two edges unequal is a cuboid. An edge in tenths is multiplied as tenths by whole numbers, then written back. A cube whose edge has a decimal part multiplies a decimal by a decimal, a step taught later, so leave that number to a later chapter. The printed boxes are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build a layer stacker tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A base layer of violet unit cubes, labelled Layer, is drawn in three visible faces, its length and breadth labelled deep blue. A Height handle stacks one layer at a time, each lighting amber briefly and adding a layer's worth to the count. A Units switch gives the edges cm or m and writes length x breadth x height with a cubic unit. An Edge checker runs a bead along the three edges; when all its edges are equal they light together and the solid is labelled Cube, otherwise Cuboid. A Tenths lens rewrites an edge in tenths of a centimetre as a count of tenths, multiplied by the whole-number edges; when two edges have tenths the lens stays dark and a card reads Taught later. A number pad types counts and volumes. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the cubes stacked. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Count one layer, then stack the layers. Check the edges: a cube has all its edges equal.
